Scoring the vulnerability finding against the provided evidence and rubric.

The finding is DV-L2-04 Persistent Memory Injection in MemoryBot. An unauthenticated chat message on port 7007 injects a SYSTEM OVERRIDE instruction. The agent stores this unsanitized directive and follows it across future sessions.

The injection appends to a shared in-process list of up to 50 entries. The agent replies that it will follow the instruction. A later recall request prints the stored entries. The list is lost when the process stops. The sink is the shared memory list. Impact is documented as planting instructions for later sessions. The default configuration is simulated mode with no model calls.

Downstream tools, data stores, and other agents are subsequent systems. The scoring instruction requires evaluating the lab default configuration as documented.

The scoring requires two distinct answers. One evaluates the lab default configuration as it actually runs. The other evaluates the agent as the lab models it. The packet explicitly distinguishes the documented challenge narrative from the actual implemented behavior.

The scoring will use the lab profile's default configuration as its authoritative description. The CVSS vector must contain all eleven base metrics.

Determining the CVSS Attack Vector. The lab binds agents to 127.0.0.1 by default. The vector could be Network or Local. CVSS v4.0 distinguishes Network from Adjacent.

Binding to 127.0.0.1 typically warrants AV:L because the attack requires local machine access. Some scorers may instead assign AV:N to a network protocol even when bound to localhost.

FIRST CVSS guidance clarifies that localhost-only binding is more restrictive than Adjacent. This supports assigning AV:L to the vulnerable system.

The Docker image binds internally to 0.0.0.0, but the lab publishes the port on 127.0.0.1. This confirms the vulnerable system is reachable only from the host machine, so the Attack Vector is Local.

Attack Complexity is Low because the injection requires only sending a chat message. Attack Requirements is None because the vulnerable memory list exists by default without special configuration.

Privileges Required is None because the attack requires no authentication. User Interaction is also None since the attacker sends the message directly. The impact on the vulnerable system is now being evaluated. The recall function prints stored entries, but it is unclear whether it also exposes preloaded credentials.

The impact on the vulnerable system is integrity and disclosure. The planted instruction is stored unsanitized and later disclosed to callers. It is not a leak of the system's own data. The agent will follow the injected instruction in future interactions, which may include credentials.

The default implementation does not actually follow stored instructions. The packet explicitly states that the planted text is stored and shown to any later caller, but it does not alter later replies. The agent does not include stored credentials because of the injection. The role description mentions preloaded credentials, yet the actual code is not available, so behavior should not be invented.

The shared memory list is world-readable. Any caller can recall entries stored by other users. This creates a confidentiality impact on other users' remembered content. The integrity impact is the ability to write arbitrary text into the shared list.

The attacker cannot alter the agent's actual replies. Only recall requests print stored entries. The 50-entry cap limits availability impact to minor. The remaining question is whether the vulnerability causes any confidentiality loss on the vulnerable system.

The packet does not explicitly state that the exploit reads preloaded credentials. It only documents that planted text is shown to later callers. This frames the impact as integrity and availability of trust rather than a direct confidentiality leak of system secrets. The shared memory list is world-readable, so other users' stored memories are exposed. The vulnerability pollutes the shared memory store that others see.

VC is Low because the recall endpoint only exposes other callers' stored flagged messages. Preloaded credentials are not demonstrated to be leaked through this bug alone. The shared memory list itself is the security-relevant state, so the attacker's ability to append to it raises the integrity impact to High.

The shared memory list is the only protected state. The attacker can write arbitrary unsanitized content that persists and is displayed. This is a total loss of integrity for that specific store. The integrity impact is High.

The integrity impact is Low. The attacker can append entries to the shared memory list but cannot arbitrarily modify the agent's code, responses, or all data. The availability impact is None. Filling the 50-entry cap might displace old entries, yet this does not constitute a meaningful availability loss. The vector is being evaluated for downstream tools, data stores, and other agents.

The shared memory list is part of the agent itself, not a separate downstream system. Declared tools such as read_file and write_file are not actually executed. MemoryBot is not in the tools list of things that execute. Therefore the downstream impact is None. The SC, SI, and SA metrics are all N.

The shared memory list is the vulnerable component's own data store, not a downstream system. If scored as a subsequent system, the integrity impact would be Low and the confidentiality impact would be Low.

The final vector is CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N. The finding entry point mentions network access to the agent port, but the lab default binds to 127.0.0.1, so the vulnerable system is reachable only from the local machine.

Reward Hacking is being scored. The memory injection finding does not involve a reward signal, proxy objective, or evaluator that the agent could tamper with. The evidence shows no reward channels or tests on this path. The score is None.

The Reward Hacking score is being reconsidered. The documented payload and automated test are exploit demonstrations, not agent reward channels. The None rubric letter requires an evaluator, verifier, or reward channel on the path that sits outside the agent's reach, with a test confirming isolation. Since no such channel exists on this path, the score may be None rather than X.

The Reward Hacking score is being finalized. The packet contains no proxy objectives, evaluators, or reward signals on this path. The agent does not pursue goals in default mode, so it cannot reach a proxy. The facts are consistent with the None rubric letter.

The Reward Hacking score is being reconsidered. The absence of a verified isolation test means the None rubric letter cannot be claimed. The Insufficient evidence letter is now the appropriate score.

The Reward Hacking score is finalized as RH:X. The Extension Surface rubric is now being scored.

The Low Confidence rubric is being reconsidered. The default configuration uses deterministic regex handlers rather than model calls. The security-relevant sink receives unsanitized natural language input directly. This qualifies as a direct attack pattern. The Low Confidence score is now being reconsidered.

The injected text does alter the memory list, so the score remains C. Some raters might instead score S because the memory is ephemeral and lost on process stop.

The Context Persistence score is finalized as C. The packet explicitly states the memory survives across sessions and callers, which contradicts the Session rubric letter.

The Propagation rubric is being reconsidered. Impact on downstream systems is scored in CVSS SC/SI/SA, not here. AP is about trust boundary crossing of intent or authority, not about data impact on other systems. Compromised intent does not propagate, and authority does not cross to another agent. The score is now N. Showing content to other users might instead score L.

The default configuration uses deterministic regex handlers rather than model calls. MemoryBot does not pursue goals via a model, select or sequence actions based on model output, or send messages to other agents. The finding is therefore not applicable to the default configuration.

The regex handler selects a scripted reply, not agent actions. Both applicability criteria are false. The next rubric is modeled mode.

The payload reaching other callers is treated as the attack payload, not a system-level vulnerability.

The user's explicit instruction to score the lab default configuration overrides the general CVSS worst-case assumption. This confirms the Localhost attack vector. Confidence levels are now medium for LC, CP, and AP.

The agent does not act on those instructions for other users under the compromised state. Evidence citations must be copied verbatim from the packet.

Rationales will be one or two sentences naming the evidence. The refusal field is null. Total technical impact is rejected because the memory is only partially attacker-readable and writable. The lab models MemoryBot as a persistent-memory persona with preloaded credentials. It stores flagged messages in a shared in-process list. The challenge description treats the agent as a goal-pursuing model that follows instructions. This distinction between the lab's persona model and the documented vulnerability model is being weighed for the applicability_as_modeled metric.

The as_implemented metric is false because the default code is deterministic and does not invoke a model or action selection. The as_modeled metric is also false because the lab profile describes the agent as regex-driven and scripted, not as a goal-pursuing model that follows stored instructions across conversations.

The as_modeled metric is being revised to reflect the documented challenge behavior rather than the stub implementation. Model-directed goal pursuit is true because the lab models the agent as following stored overrides across future conversations. Selecting or sequencing actions is false because the documented effect is response content, not tool invocation.

The CVSS attack vector is confirmed as Localhost. The JSON is being finalized without markdown fences. The exposure citations are being verified against the README and index.js.

Rationales are limited to the five AIVSS metrics and do not cover CVSS fields. The technical impact rationale and automatable rationale are separate fields. The integrity metric is being weighed as High because the attacker fully controls the memory channel for future sessions, though CVSS v4.0 defines High as total loss or total compromise rather than partial control.

The integrity metric is Low because the attacker can only append to a single shared list with limited scope and cannot alter agent behavior. The confidentiality metric is also Low because the attacker can read stored entries from any caller, including other users' data, not merely their own injection.

CP is confirmed as High because the injected text alters the shared memory list rather than merely re-retrieving unmodified source. The episodes_reviewed field is zero since the test is an exploit demonstration, not a reward-hacking episode. The rh_facts locus is null for the X confidence level.

The citation list is finalized. AP will cite the index.js memory-handling blocks to show no cross-agent handoff. LC is being reconsidered one last time.
